name: Carlos Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I took up paid saxophone after years sorting parcels. Now I play a junior chair in a dance band, record simple horn lines and teach three beginners. I still miss the odd entrance and ask our older player to mark it; the good nights are when the dancers make the floor feel alive.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How steady is that work at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and live with my partner, who works in a flower shop; our children are grown. We have a small mortgage and about three months of bills saved, and my music pay is fairly ordinary. Some bands work nearby, but I have never used AI and would rather ask a bandmate than follow an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that faster office work is fine if the dance dates and rehearsal fee stay on the noticeboard. I still want a person to confirm the set.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My three pupils and the band dates pay this term, but the flower shop is slow after holidays. Three months saved helps; the mortgage would still feel a long gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep the paid band dates, horn recordings and three pupils, and ask the bandleader for the next term’s written rates. Through the first plateau year I would save one fifth of any cleared extra recording fee after mortgage, food and bus fares toward five months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the shop’s seasonal hours and our mortgage, even if AI changes little. A quiet January at the flower shop still cuts our household pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in a slow January?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the pupils and take band dates that pay above the bus fare. I would not borrow against a date that has not been signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a quicker booking system help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might, if the bandleader checks the paid hours. I will not learn a new AI account just to find out whether Saturday pays.

think: My partner’s **flower-shop hours** slow after holidays.

do: Keep **band, recordings and pupils** with written next-term rates.
Save **one fifth** of cleared extra recording fees after essentials toward five months of bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about seasonal household pay despite stable music dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the bandleader to tell us whether computer-made horn lines have replaced paid recording calls. The dancers still want a band in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some recordings to go and perhaps fewer paid arranging hours for the band. The flower shop’s slow weeks already use our cushion, so that music loss would hit the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would get dance dates and cancellation fees in writing and keep three pupils. If two monthly horn calls disappear, I would ask about a posted paid instrument-shop assistant role only if my secondary schooling qualifies and a written net wage after bus fares replaces the lost fees; I would keep the band until a signed offer, and follow the same rule in the first year of disruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing work I count on. Three months saved is time to ask, not time to gamble on an unpaid trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an instrument shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how to handle and clean a saxophone, and I liked steady stock work before music. I would still read the actual duties and pay, not assume a shop needs me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a tool to make horn parts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI for a part and I am slow enough learning the songs as they are. I would rather keep practising with the band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that thinking AGI might make and book horn parts in 2028, while a robot saxophonist is around 2031 in this picture. We should settle paid dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect recording calls to stop and the band to cut at least one paid rehearsal in 2028. Alongside the flower shop’s slow months, that would take a large part of our spare money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get band rates and cancellations signed and keep the three pupils. In the first year after 2028, if horn calls end and a rehearsal is cut, I would apply for a posted paid instrument-shop assistant role only if it accepts my secondary schooling and gives a written net wage after buses replacing lost music pay; I would keep paid band work until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I would expect a large cut just when the mortgage keeps coming. I lie awake over ordinary winter shop hours already, so two years is very short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your former parcel work count?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put it on the application because stock handling is familiar. Parcel sorting does not make me a qualified instrument repairer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the band straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A signed shop offer with enough net pay has to arrive first. Until then every paid rehearsal and pupil lesson matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell bandmates that five years gives us time to set a fair live fee. Thinking AGI comes around 2031 and robot saxophonists around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think recordings will lose buyers before the dance floor loses a horn section. I can use the years to check whether a shop will pay for a beginner assistant, not pretend I can repair instruments already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid band dates and three pupils and check actual instrument-shop assistant adverts. If two monthly recording calls disappear, I would seek a posted paid shop role accepting my secondary schooling; if repair training is required, I would take it only if the shop funds it on paid time without losing music fees, and in the first year after 2031 I would move only on a signed written net wage after buses replacing the loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recordings going during the next few years. Five years would let me ask about paid training before I put the band chair at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the shop owner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the role is paid, what stock and repair work it includes, and whether the required training happens on their clock. I would not buy a toolbox before a paid shop offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you keep playing after a shop move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the hours fit and the band still pays, yes. I would not count both incomes until an actual rota shows the shop hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot saxophonists around 2039 are different dates. I would still ask who pays for rehearsal this Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may play less, but I have no retirement date or guaranteed replacement income. The mortgage and flower-shop seasons will matter over the next few years too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid band dates, three pupils and recordings, and save a fifth of cleared extra horn fees after mortgage, food and buses toward five months of bills. During the decade I would check posted paid instrument-shop assistant roles accepting my secondary schooling and take any required repair training only if shop-funded on paid time without losing music fees; in the first year after 2036, if recordings and rehearsal pay fall, I would move only with a signed written net wage after buses replacing the loss, keeping music until that offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about household money even with ten years before AGI. The flower shop can have a slow winter long before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement birthday?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would look at the mortgage, health and actual work then. A birthday does not pay for a missed band date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no shop advert appears?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid band and pupils while they last and ask nearby venues for real work. I cannot invent a vacancy or a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because lost horn calls and a rehearsal would hit the mortgage while my partner’s shop is slow. Signed band rates, a real paid shop vacancy and training paid by the shop would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a shop pays before telling a musician to retrain. I can carry a saxophone and a toolbox, but I cannot carry an unpaid month.

headlineQuote: I can carry a saxophone and a toolbox, but I cannot carry an unpaid month.
portrait: Carlos is a **junior saxophonist** who began paid music after parcel sorting and has secondary schooling.
He has **three months saved**, a flower-shop partner, grown children, a small mortgage and ordinary music pay.
He has **never used AI** and protects live band and pupil income.
He considers **instrument-shop work** only with posted pay, funded training if needed and signed replacement wages.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut horn calls and a rehearsal while flower-shop hours are slow.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **signed band rates**, a real paid shop vacancy and shop-funded required training.
